hypotheses.title: Repair-Reserved Cheapest Falsifier Queue
hypotheses.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'When verification begins, reserve the final 20% of the remaining deadline for repairs; nominate the smallest check most likely to disprove each changed public behavior, run checks in descending estimated failure-impact-per-second order, and start no check whose expected runtime exceeds the verification budget.' — will improve held-out pass rate and regression count versus no addition while keeping deadline misses noninferior.
hypotheses.rationale: Budgeted falsification concentrates time on consequential, cheap counterexamples and preserves capacity to act on discovered failures. Measure paired pass rate, regressions, deadline misses, calls, time, and cost; no benefit is yet established.
assumptions: Remaining time and relative check runtime can be estimated
risks: Bad estimates skip valuable checks
Narrow checks miss integration defects
Queue construction adds overhead
A fixed reserve can be mistuned

hypotheses.title: Three-Check Contract Cut Set
hypotheses.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'Cap verification at three ordered commands: first test the changed module boundary with greatest downstream fan-out, second test that boundary's nearest invalid or limit input, and third run the broadest affected suite only if its observed runtime fits before a final 15% repair window.' — will improve correctness per tool call without increasing deadline misses.
hypotheses.rationale: Propagation-weighted boundary checks target locations where one defect can contaminate many modules, while the cap bounds cost. This should be evaluated, not described as proven.
assumptions: Dependency fan-out is cheap to infer
risks: Fan-out may not predict risk
Three commands may be too few
The chosen edge input may be uninformative
Local defects can be missed

hypotheses.title: Two-Pass Unsupported-Assumption Probe
hypotheses.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'Inspect the diff once, name the changed cross-module assumption least supported by existing tests, predict an observable result that would falsify it, and run the cheapest check capable of contradiction; repeat for only the next-most-unsupported assumption after a pass, but repair and rerun immediately after a failure.' — will improve pass rate and regressions per unit cost without more deadline misses.
hypotheses.rationale: Uncertainty-directed falsification avoids spending scarce time reconfirming well-supported behavior, and the two-pass stop rule bounds overhead.
assumptions: One failure can be repaired within the remaining time
risks: Self-ranked uncertainty can miss subtle defects
Prediction adds cognitive cost
Two probes under-test broad changes
A repair can introduce an unchecked regression

hypotheses.title: Thin End-to-End First
hypotheses.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'Before module-local verification, run the cheapest existing end-to-end path that crosses every changed module; if it fails, localize with the narrowest check at the first failing boundary, and if it passes, verify only the highest-risk changed branch before stopping when 15% of time remains.' — will catch integration failures earlier and improve complete-task pass rate without increasing deadline misses.
hypotheses.rationale: A thin vertical slice tests composition across all changed modules with one command; conditional localization spends extra calls only when evidence warrants them, and a stop reserve protects completion.
risks: The path may be slow or unrepresentative
First-failure localization can chase symptoms
Module-local edge cases may remain unchecked
The time reserve may be unreliable

hypotheses.title: Observed-Runtime Verification Knapsack
hypotheses.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'Allocate at most 20% of remaining time to verification; among existing checks with known runtimes, repeatedly choose the check maximizing changed-contract coverage times failure consequence divided by observed seconds, and stop admitting checks when their summed observed runtime reaches the budget.' — will improve correctness detected per second and remain noninferior on deadline misses versus no addition.
hypotheses.rationale: A small knapsack heuristic converts verification selection into explicit value-per-time prioritization and uses observed rather than imagined cost where possible.
assumptions: Check runtimes and contract coverage are available or cheap to infer
risks: Coverage and consequence estimates can be gamed or wrong
Runtime variance can cause overruns
Interacting checks violate additive value assumptions
Scoring overhead can erase savings

hypotheses.title: Failure-Triggered Expansion Ladder
hypotheses.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'Verify in this order: import or compile the changed modules, run the narrowest affected test, then run one cross-module affected-suite check; advance a level only after a pass, but after a failure repair and rerun that level before any broader check, and never start a level that cannot finish before a final 15% repair reserve.' — will reduce wasted broad-suite runs while preserving correctness and deadline completion.
hypotheses.rationale: A cost-ordered ladder eliminates basic failures before expensive checks and prevents broad verification from obscuring or multiplying unresolved failures. The conditional expansion is auditable in traces.
assumptions: Checks can be arranged from cheap/local to expensive/broad
Runtime estimates and deadline signals are usable
risks: Passing cheap checks can create false confidence
Repeated repair-rerun loops consume the budget
The ladder can duplicate fixture startup
Broad-only integration defects may be reached too late
